description: The Andromeda group consists of five members with a shared passion for science, technology, music, and accessibility. Inspired by the myth of Andromeda and the concept of liberation, we aim—through our project, Earth Jukebox—to break down barriers to accessing scientific information. We transform NASA data and visualizations into an interactive, multisensory experience, enabling everyone—including the blind and visually impaired—to hear and understand the changes occurring on planet Earth.
summary: Our Earth Jukebox is an interactive web application that lets people hear the air around them. It retrieves real NASA GEOS-CF atmospheric-model data for NO₂, PM2.5 and CO₂, shows it on a map and timeline with NASA GIBS satellite imagery, and turns it into music generated live in the browser. Five rules link the data to sound: higher concentrations raise the pitch, faster changes speed up the tempo, wider affected areas add instrument layers, trends shape the melody, and spatial patterns shape timbre and stereo. As pollution rises and spreads, the music climbs higher and grows fuller. A Frame-to-Sound feature also sonifies frames and all three gases become music from the data, and users can upload their own music to be reshaped by the data. The map, timeline, statistics and audio stay synchronized, missing data becomes silence rather than invented values, and screen-reader narration describes what is playing. The music arises from the data itself, and by turning air pollution into sound, Earth Jukebox opens Earth science to blind and low-vision users and helps everyone feel and understand the air we breathe.
details:
What it does. Earth Jukebox is our web app that downloads real NASA GEOS-CF data for NO₂, PM2.5 and CO₂ and plays it as live music, in sync with a map and timeline. The full version runs with a small Python server. We also provide a single HTML file with real NASA data built in, which plays directly in any browser with no installation, and a folder of sample music that users can upload to hear their own track reshaped by the pollution data.

Benefits and impact. People can hear air quality, not only see it. Screen-reader narration opens the data to blind and low-vision users.

Tools. A Python 3.10+ server (standard library only), HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the browser, the Web Audio API, Leaflet and Chart.js. No special hardware or API key.

Creativity. The music is generated from the numbers, not from a background track; even a user’s own song is reshaped by the data.

Factors considered. Scientific honesty: missing data stays silent, data versions are never mixed, and alerts are indicative only. Some of the music are played by our own team members, and our slogan is "Listen - Understand and Breathe"
dataRefs: NASA GEOS-CF (GMAO / NCCS OPeNDAP) – NO₂, PM2.5 and CO₂ model data that our app turns into music
NASA GIBS – daily satellite imagery and context layers (MODIS, VIIRS, OCO-2/3) shown on our map
NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) and its API – videos and metadata for our in-app gallery
Earth Information Center (EIC) Content Database – challenge visualizations shown in our gallery
DYAMOND Global Carbon Dioxide – video frames converted into sound by our Frame to  Sound feature
NASA Data Sonifications (Hubble & Chandra) – inspiration for mapping data to pitch and loudness
projectRefs: Leaflet – open-source library that displays our map and pollution layer
Chart.js – open-source library that draws our statistics charts
Web Audio API (MDN) – browser standard we use to generate the music live and export WAV
OpenStreetMap Nominatim – country and city search
U.S. EPA AQI Basics – reference levels for our indicative NO₂ and PM2.5 alerts
WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) – guideline values used as an alert option
Accessible Oceans (WHOI) – model for designing data sound with blind and low-vision users
Russo et al. (2024), Nature Reviews Earth & Environment – scientific basis for sonifying Earth-science data
